  All of mirt, with tidy outputs, ggplot2 figures and one-call reports, so

---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

mirtverse sits on top of mirt and leaves estimation alone. What it adds is
the work around a model: Tidy data frames for your pipeline, ggplot2 figures
you can restyle, and reports you can attach to a paper.

## Your path in three steps

**1. Keep using mirt, get tidy outputs.** Any `mirt()` model works:

```r
library(mirtverse)
mod <- mirt(data, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
tidy(mod)       # one row per parameter, with standard errors
glance(mod)     # one row of fit statistics
augment(mod)    # person scores added to the data
```

**2. Make figures for the paper.** Each `gg_*()` function returns a ggplot2
object, and `theme_mirtverse()` gives a clean journal style:

```r
gg_trace(mod, which.items = 1:4)
gg_wright(mod)
gg_q3(mod)          # local dependence
```

See the [Gallery](gallery.html) for every figure type with its code.

**3. Go beyond the standard model.** Response-time models, DIF in one call,
and explanatory item models from item text:

```r
fit_rt(mod, rt)                      # joint responses and response times
dif(data, group = group)             # DIF with effect sizes
d <- merge(itemtext, item_features(itemtext))
predict_difficulty(d, c("words", "max_digits", "decimals"))  # difficulty from item text
```

## Citing

Please cite both mirt and mirtverse. `citation("mirtverse")` returns both
references; the [authors page](../authors.html#citation) has them too, and
the book can be cited separately
([10.5281/zenodo.23885605](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23885605)).
